newsitem.title: USA: Mass. Electric to cut rates under plan.
newsitem.headline: Mass. Electric to cut rates under plan.

text.p: Massachusetts Electric Co said it would would cut rates by 10 percent under a proposal by the utility and Mass. Attorney General Scott Harshbarger to restructure the state's electric industry.

John Rowe, Chief Executive of New England Electric System, which owns Massachusetts Electric, said under the plan, all customers would get at least a 10 percent discount beginning in 1998. In exchange, Massachusetts Electric would charge 2.8 cents per kilowatt hour over three years to recover stranded costs under the restructuring, Rowe said.

The charge would be amortized over a 12 year period and cut from 2.8 cents "fairly quickly" to recover about $3 billion in stranded costs, said Rick Sergel, senior vice president of Massachusetts Electric.
"Ten percent out of our revenues is a lot of blood and we're willing to risk that in order to get fair treatment in our sunken costs," Rowe said.

Harshbarger will present the plan, called "consumers first", to other members of the electric industry in the next few weeks before filing the proposal with the the Mass. Department of Public Utilities (DPU), which submitted its own proposals to restructure the industry.

However, the Competitive Power Coalition of New England, which represents independent power producers and power marketers, objected to the "backroom deal" and were never contacted about the proposed plan, said spokesman John Michael Kennedy.

Under the proposal, all customers of investor-owned utilities would be free to choose a new supplier of electricity beginning in 1998. Utilities and suppliers would competitively bid against each other to supply power. Under a "standard offer" option, all users would be guaranteed a savings of at least 10 percent off current prices even if they do not enter the competitive market immediately.

"If my plan is implemented across the state, it would mean a total savings to homeowners and business customers of at least three billion dollars," Harshbarger said. "I hope that this is the way the state is going to go," he added.
The DPU and other utilities were not available to comment.
Rowe said under a competitive market, rates could actually be reduced by more than 15 percent, but the utility would guarantee at least a 10 percent cut.

Sergel said Massachusetts Electric would sell 15 percent of its assets, including fossil and hydro generating plants, if the plan were implemented. He said many buyers have expressed interest in the assets, but no firm offers have been made.
